name: eRPC
baseline: conventional kernel TCP/UDP socket-based RPC (and specialized RDMA-only systems like FaSST/HERD)
workload: Small (32-byte) and large (8MB) RPC calls over Ethernet/InfiniBand/RoCE NICs, plus a 3-way Raft replication port, on commodity DPDK-capable or Mellanox NICs
claimed_speedup: up to 10 million 32-byte RPCs/sec on one CPU core (60-80M RPCs/sec per NIC); 75 Gbps on one connection for 8MB RPCs; 2.3us round-trip RPC latency over UDP/Ethernet; 5.3us for 3-way Raft replication
hardware: Mellanox CX3-CX5 or DPDK-capable NICs (exact CPU model not stated on the pages opened this session; full details are in the NSDI'19 paper PDF, which could not be text-extracted via WebFetch)
tradeoffs: Requires DPDK/RDMA-capable NICs and huge pages; a binary RPC library, not an HTTP-semantics server (no TLS/HTTP parsing); app must integrate its session/event-loop model
caveats: NSDI'19 paper's own baseline is conventional TCP/UDP RPC and other specialized RDMA systems, not nginx/Boost.Beast/actix-web/uvloop directly, so baseline_in_list=false; exact hardware CPU model and compiler flags could not be confirmed from the pages opened (WebFetch could not extract readable text from the PDF); category fit is RPC-over-network rather than literal HTTP serving, included because the assignment's own starting query explicitly targets kernel-bypass high-performance server research. Authors now point new users to a successor project, microsoft/machnet, for DPDK-based messaging (checked; 162 stars, MIT, active, but its README states only an absolute number '750K RPS at 61us P99.9' with no named baseline comparison, so it does not itself qualify under rule 1).
found_via: arXiv/USENIX query 'eRPC general purpose RPC library' -> https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi19/presentation/kalia and https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi19-kalia.pdf

name: IX (protected dataplane OS)
baseline: Linux kernel networking stack (and unnamed user-space network stacks of its era)
workload: A widely-deployed in-memory key-value store (memcached-class) served natively on IX vs. on Linux
claimed_speedup: up to 3.6x throughput improvement and more than 2x reduction in tail latency, per the OSDI'14 paper's own abstract text
license: Custom-named 'IX Open Source License' whose text is verbatim MIT (not SPDX-registered under that name)
tradeoffs: Dedicates full hardware threads and NIC queues to dataplane instances (spin-polling), trading CPU sharing flexibility for latency; research-grade, unmaintained since 2017; needs kernel-bypass-capable NIC setup
caveats: Exact CPU model, compiler and flags were not confirmed on the abstract page opened this session (the full PDF's text could not be extracted); the benchmarked workload is a key-value store, not literally HTTP, though it targets the same 'fast networked server' job nginx/actix-web/etc. perform, which the assignment's own starting query (kernel bypass) explicitly invites
found_via: arXiv query 'kernel bypass HTTP server throughput latency' -> https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi14/technical-sessions/presentation/belay

name: Shenango
baseline: ZygOS (a state-of-the-art kernel-bypass network stack) and standard Linux kernel networking
workload: Memcached and synthetic microsecond-scale request/response workloads mixing latency-sensitive and batch applications, reallocating CPU cores every 5us
claimed_speedup: Per the NSDI'19 abstract page: 'Shenango achieves tail latency and throughput comparable to ZygOS ... but can linearly trade latency-sensitive application throughput for batch processing application throughput, vastly increasing CPU efficiency.' No single numeric multiplier is stated on that page.
tradeoffs: Requires DPDK and a dedicated IOKernel scheduling process; kernel-bypass core reallocation adds operational complexity
caveats: The repository's own README states 'This repository is no longer maintained' and directs users to the successor shenango/caladan; marked abandoned here despite a 2024 push because the maintainers themselves declared it superseded. No exact numeric multiplier for the ZygOS/Linux comparison was found on the pages opened this session, only the qualitative claim quoted above. The successor, shenango/caladan (200 stars, Apache-2.0, actively pushed as of 2026-09-25), was checked but its NSDI'20 paper page 404'd and its README states no quantified comparison, so Caladan itself is not reported here as a separate entry.

name: Demikernel
workload: Redis ported to Demikernel, run over three backends (Linux kernel sockets, RDMA kernel-bypass, DPDK kernel-bypass) on CloudLab with a 25Gb network and Mellanox CX-4 NICs
claimed_speedup: Per the project author's blog post: the Linux kernel interface path accounts for ~30% of Redis request latency, and switching to RDMA/DPDK kernel-bypass removes another ~30%, i.e. the kernel+its interface together account for roughly 60% of total latency in that benchmark
tradeoffs: Project explicitly labeled a research prototype with 'no guarantees'; requires DPDK/RDMA hardware for the kernel-bypass LibOSes (catnip); Linux-socket LibOS (catnap) has no bypass benefit by itself
caveats: This is a first-party blog post (by the project's own researcher), not the peer-reviewed SOSP'21 paper text itself (doi:10.1145/3477132.3483569 is paywalled and could not be fetched this session), so tier is capped at C; the reported percentages are relative latency-breakdown figures, not a single 'Nx faster' multiplier vs a named production baseline like nginx
found_via: arXiv query 'Demikernel kernel bypass datapath' (no results) -> GitHub README linked blog post http://irenezhang.net/blog/2019/05/21/demikernel.html

name: FlexTOE
baseline: Linux host TCP stack, TAS (TCP Acceleration as an OS Service), and the Chelsio Terminator hardware TCP offload engine
workload: Memcached and RPC microbenchmarks on an Agilio-CX40 SmartNIC, plus single-connection RPC throughput on x86 and BlueField hosts
claimed_speedup: Per the paper's own abstract: Memcached scales up to 38% better on FlexTOE than on TAS; saves up to 81% of host CPU cycles vs. Chelsio; cuts 99.99th-percentile RPC RTT by 3.2x vs. Chelsio and by 50% vs. TAS; improves single-connection RPC throughput up to 2.4x on x86 and 4x on BlueField
hardware: Netronome Agilio-CX40 SmartNIC; x86 and BlueField hosts (exact host CPU model not stated in the abstract)
tradeoffs: Requires a Netronome Agilio SmartNIC; programmability via C/eBPF/XDP adds development complexity vs. a plain sockets server; unmaintained since 2022
caveats: One of its named baselines, TAS (tcp-acceleration-service/tas), is itself unreleased since 2020 and its EuroSys'19 paper page returned HTTP 403 (ACM DL) this session, so TAS's own standalone claims could not be independently verified and TAS is not reported as its own entry; FlexTOE's numbers above come from its own arXiv preprint abstract (peer-reviewed at NSDI'22), which is openly accessible, but exact host CPU model and compiler flags are not stated there
found_via: arXiv query 'TAS TCP Acceleration OS Service Kaufmann' -> https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.10919 (FlexTOE: Flexible TCP Offload with Fine-Grained Parallelism)
